cards.scenario: Master account admins must stop or terminate resources in Dev and Test accounts.
cards.ok: IAM users in master account; cross-account admin roles created in Dev and Test accounts.
cards.bad: Create the cross-account role in the master account instead.
cards.why: Cross-account role must live in the target accounts; consolidated billing grants no resource access.

cards.scenario: Only owning business unit may terminate its EC2, EKS, Aurora resources across accounts.
cards.ok: Organizations OUs per business unit + IAM role in production account with resource-level terminate permission.
cards.bad: Service Control Policy in production account granting terminate access to the OUs.
cards.why: SCPs only limit permissions and never grant access; IAM roles grant cross-account access.

cards.scenario: Only Solutions Architects may stop or terminate production instances (select two).
cards.ok: Remove developers' terminate permission from their IAM role + tag production and deny terminate by tag.
cards.bad: Require MFA in developers' IAM policy before deleting EC2 instances.
cards.why: MFA still allows the terminate action; the fix is removing or denying the permission.

cards.scenario: Let signed-in corporate users manage AWS without separate IAM users.
cards.ok: SAML 2.0 on-premises IdP federation via STS and IAM Identity Center for console access.
cards.bad: Use AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the SAML 2.0 IdP.
cards.why: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is for web identity providers; SAML federation is the on-premises fit.

cards.scenario: EC2 web server must upload photos to S3 securely.
cards.ok: IAM role on instance; temporary credentials fetched from instance metadata.
cards.bad: IAM service role attached, but credentials retrieved from instance userdata.
cards.why: Credentials come from instance metadata, not userdata; SCPs only restrict and IAM users leak keys.

cards.scenario: Employees use existing Windows AD password for SSO to AWS; extend AD.
cards.ok: AWS Directory Service (Managed Microsoft AD) with trust to existing AD.
cards.bad: IAM Identity Center with new users and groups plus Organizations.
cards.why: Trust with Managed Microsoft AD extends the existing domain; Identity Center alone does not.

cards.scenario: Mobile photo app, millions of users, access S3 most securely.
cards.ok: IAM role plus STS AssumeRole temporary credentials on each app open, held in memory.
cards.bad: Generate long-term credentials with STS and store in the app.
cards.why: Mobile apps need short-lived credentials; STS credentials are temporary and IAM users leak keys.

cards.scenario: Authenticate against on-premises LDAP; each user reaches only own S3 bucket (two).
cards.ok: Authenticate against LDAP, then assume role or broker calls STS for federated credentials.
cards.bad: Use LDAP credentials to log in to IAM, then use temporary credentials.
cards.why: LDAP credentials cannot log into IAM; STS issues credentials after LDAP authentication.

cards.scenario: SAML 2.0 federation partly works; what to verify (select three).
cards.ok: Role trust names SAML provider; IdP maps roles; AssumeRoleWithSAML gets ARNs plus assertion.
cards.bad: User IAM policy allows SAML federation.
cards.why: Permissions come from the mapped IAM role, not an individual user's policy.

cards.scenario: App instances access DynamoDB via CloudFormation without exposing credentials.
cards.ok: IAM role, referenced by the instance's instance profile property.
cards.bad: IAM role ARN stored in SSM parameter, then referenced by instance profile.
cards.why: Role supplies temporary credentials; an SSM parameter holding the ARN adds nothing.

cards.scenario: Replace unavailable NAT instances: better availability and bandwidth, minimal admin effort.
cards.ok: Managed NAT gateway with Elastic IP; private route table points internet traffic to it.
cards.bad: Two large NAT instances in separate public subnets, routed from private subnet.
cards.why: Highly available but you still manage both instances; NAT gateway is managed and has more bandwidth.

cards.scenario: Two EC2 instances in different subnets must communicate; track security configuration history.
cards.ok: AWS Config for configuration history + NACL and security group rules allowing app-to-database traffic.
cards.bad: Systems Manager to track historical security configuration changes.
cards.why: Config records configuration history; Systems Manager does not. NACLs and security groups control subnet traffic.

cards.scenario: Improve availability and load balancing of web tier with minimal human intervention (select two).
cards.ok: ALB with Route 53 alias record + Route 53 multivalue answer record listing web server IPs.
cards.bad: Load balancer fronted by a Route 53 non-alias record.
cards.why: Pointing to an ALB DNS name requires an alias record, not a non-alias record.

cards.scenario: Instances must resolve both VPC endpoints and custom Managed AD domain (select two).
cards.ok: Route 53 outbound endpoint + forwarding rule for the AD domain to the domain controllers.
cards.bad: Route 53 inbound endpoint with AmazonProvidedDNS as VPC resolver.
cards.why: Inbound endpoints take queries into the VPC; forwarding to the AD servers needs an outbound endpoint.

cards.scenario: Centralized controlled egress for thousands of accounts; account admins keep route-table autonomy.
cards.ok: Shared Transit Gateway with spoke VPCs and a central VPC using Gateway Load Balancer + firewalls.
cards.bad: Transit VPC connecting each account's VPC by VPN, with firewall appliances.
cards.why: VPN connections between VPCs are unnecessary and slower than the AWS backbone with Transit Gateway.

cards.scenario: Restrict EC2 internet access to specific package URLs only.
cards.ok: Forward web proxy in VPC with URL-based rules; remove default routes.
cards.bad: Network ACL rules allowing only package destinations, implicit deny elsewhere.
cards.why: NACLs and security groups cannot filter by URL; a proxy can.

cards.scenario: Clients cannot send logs via PrivateLink to NLB-fronted EC2 (select two).
cards.ok: NACL allows NLB subnets both ways + EC2 security group allows NLB security group.
cards.bad: NACL allows interface endpoint to and from the logging subnets.
cards.why: Targets see NLB node IPs as source, not the client or endpoint.

cards.scenario: Peer VPC-A to one DB IP in VPC-B plus all of VPC-C; CIDRs overlap.
cards.ok: VPC-A static routes: 10.0.0.77/32 via B peering, 10.0.0.0/16 via C; return routes.
cards.bad: Route VPC-B CIDR 10.0.0.0/24 and VPC-C 10.0.0.0/24 plus NACL filtering.
cards.why: Longest prefix match sends the /32 to B; everything else in the /16 goes to C.

cards.scenario: Highly available in us-west-1; passive backup site in us-east-1.
cards.ok: Duplicate ALB + Auto Scaling in us-east-1; Route 53 failover routing with health checks.
cards.bad: Same two regional stacks with separate Route 53 records, health checks, no failover policy.
cards.why: Passive DR needs failover routing; plain separate records with health checks would treat both regions as active.

cards.scenario: Static content differs by device type; reduce EC2 load and improve response time.
cards.ok: S3 origin behind CloudFront with Lambda@Edge parsing User-Agent to serve device-specific content.
cards.bad: CloudFront configured to deliver different content based on the User-Agent header natively.
cards.why: Lambda@Edge applies the device logic at the edge for every request, offloading EC2 instances.

cards.scenario: Serve files to one California client only, block direct S3 access (two).
cards.ok: S3 pre-signed URLs, or CloudFront signed URLs with OAC; remove other S3 read access.
cards.bad: CloudFront signed cookies with HTTPS.
cards.why: Signed cookies suit many files; direct S3 URLs must also be closed.

cards.scenario: Serve S3 static and ALB dynamic content only through CloudFront (select two).
cards.ok: OAC for S3 bucket + CloudFront custom header, WAF web ACL on the ALB.
cards.bad: NACL on ALB subnets allowing CloudFront only.
cards.why: CloudFront IPs are not fixed, so a NACL cannot reliably restrict the ALB.

cards.scenario: Partners must access S3 files only through CloudFront, never S3 URLs.
cards.ok: CloudFront origin access control (OAC); S3 bucket permits only the OAC.
cards.bad: Bucket policy naming the CloudFront distribution ID as Principal.
cards.why: OAC gives CloudFront exclusive S3 read access; other approaches leave direct URLs open.

cards.scenario: Blog entries: frequent early updates, rarely read later; improve load times with CloudFront.
cards.ok: One S3 bucket partitioned by submission month, CloudFront restricted to it.
cards.bad: CloudFront with minimum TTL of 0 and query string forwarding.
cards.why: Minimum TTL 0 reloads from origin even for unchanged old content.

cards.scenario: Require HTTPS viewer-to-CloudFront on custom domain (select two).
cards.ok: ACM-provided SSL/TLS certificate + longest practical Cache-Control max-age.
cards.bad: Import third-party certificate into a private S3 bucket.
cards.why: Certificates belong in ACM (or the IAM store), not S3.

cards.scenario: Instances in one AZ receive no ALB requests despite multi-AZ Auto Scaling.
cards.ok: The AZ was never associated with (enabled on) the Application Load Balancer.
cards.bad: Instances must be manually added in each AZ before they receive traffic.
cards.why: Targets in an AZ get no traffic unless that AZ is enabled on the load balancer.

cards.scenario: ML defect detection must keep working when factory internet is down.
cards.ok: IoT Greengrass on local server runs SageMaker-trained model inference, calls the Linux API via components.
cards.bad: SageMaker Edge Manager deploying the model directly onto the IP cameras.
cards.why: Greengrass runs ML inference locally and offline against a local server and its API.

cards.scenario: Stateless fleet at 90-100% CPU peaks, average 20%; cost-optimal over three years.
cards.ok: Auto Scaling group on NLB, min 5 and max 30, Reserved Instances for 5.
cards.bad: ASG min 15, max 25, Reserved Instances for 15 instances.
cards.why: Reserve only the baseline; a max of 25 leaves no scaling headroom for peaks.

cards.scenario: What does this CloudFormation SNS topic snippet do with Fn::GetAtt?
cards.ok: Creates SNS topic with subscription using the SQS queue's ARN attribute from logical name TutorialsDojoQueue.
cards.bad: Creates SNS topic and also invokes creation of the TutorialsDojoQueue SQS queue.
cards.why: GetAtt only reads the Arn of an existing template resource; it does not create the queue.

cards.scenario: Self-service SageMaker notebooks for non-expert data scientists, preconfigured KMS key, least overhead.
cards.ok: CloudFormation template with simple Mappings published as an AWS Service Catalog portfolio.
cards.bad: CloudFormation template shared by uploading it to an S3 bucket.
cards.why: Service Catalog gives governed self-service; raw template distribution exposes complexity and lacks managed portfolio access.

cards.scenario: Migrate Oracle RAC; automate OS patching and scheduled backups with least effort.
cards.ok: Oracle RAC on multi-AZ EC2, Data Lifecycle Manager EBS snapshots, SSM Patch Manager.
cards.bad: Migrate to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ failover for the RAC cluster.
cards.why: RDS for Oracle does not support RAC, so it must run on EC2.

cards.scenario: Non-urgent Lambda replication must not exhaust regional concurrency for critical functions.
cards.ok: Set a reserved concurrency limit on the replication function and monitor Throttles.
cards.bad: Raise the function timeout to 5 minutes so it waits for concurrency.
cards.why: A timeout does not queue throttled invocations; reserved concurrency caps usage.

cards.scenario: Versioned, repeatable infrastructure as code plus CDN for public apps.
cards.ok: CloudFormation for infrastructure, CloudFront as CDN.
cards.bad: CloudFront as CDN with Elastic Beanstalk managing the architecture.
cards.why: Beanstalk cannot manage infrastructure as code or version whole stacks; CloudFormation can.

cards.scenario: Scalable, highly available global issue tracker.
cards.ok: CloudFormation, Auto Scaling across AZs behind ELB, CloudFront, RDS Multi-AZ.
cards.bad: Auto Scaling of Spot instances, CloudFront, RDS with Read Replicas.
cards.why: Spot is unfit for steady load; Read Replicas give limited availability versus Multi-AZ.

cards.scenario: Redeploy voting app after stack deletion keeping photos and DB data.
cards.ok: S3 DeletionPolicy Retain, RDS DeletionPolicy Snapshot.
cards.bad: DeletionPolicy Retain on both S3 and RDS.
cards.why: Retaining RDS keeps a running idle database costing money; snapshot is cheaper.

cards.scenario: Stateless web and app tiers handling unpredictable load; HA and scale.
cards.ok: Stateless Auto Scaling, ElastiCache Serverless, CloudWatch, RDS Multi-AZ with read replicas.
cards.bad: Stateful instances in Auto Scaling group with RDS Multi-AZ.
cards.why: Stateless scales horizontally; Multi-AZ alone gives availability, not read performance.

cards.scenario: Stateless REST service, minimal cost and operational overhead, authenticated requests, persistent metadata.
cards.ok: API Gateway + per-resource Lambda, Cognito user pools, DynamoDB Auto Scaling, S3 presigned URLs.
cards.bad: Fargate behind ALB with custom authenticator, proxying S3 data through the service.
cards.why: Serverless API Gateway with Cognito is cheaper and lower-ops than Fargate with a custom authenticator.

cards.scenario: Cost-effective searchable site over 20-50 TB scanned files, running three-plus years.
cards.ok: S3 Standard storage + Amazon OpenSearch Service for search, website on Elastic Beanstalk.
cards.bad: Use S3 alone for storing and searching via native search.
cards.why: S3 has no effective native search; add OpenSearch for the query function.

cards.scenario: Cost-effective push notifications to 2 million-plus iOS/Android users within a minute.
cards.ok: SQS queue, EC2 fleet reading DynamoDB, SNS Mobile Push to send offers.
cards.bad: Lambda over SQS with Aurora Serverless, publishing to SNS topics via SMS.
cards.why: SNS Mobile Push is the push-notification channel; SMS to registered phone numbers is wrong and costlier.

cards.scenario: On-premises Kafka output to AWS: near-real-time, consistent high-performance network (select three).
cards.ok: Kinesis Producer Library from EC2 + Direct Connect + Lambda and API Gateway WebSocket with @connections.
cards.bad: Site-to-Site VPN from the data center to the VPC.
cards.why: VPN rides the internet and gives no consistent performance; Direct Connect does.

cards.scenario: Enrich 500 IoT sensors' data into S3 data lake within 20 minutes, cheapest and scalable.
cards.ok: IoT Basic Ingest to Data Firehose with Lambda enrichment, 300-second buffer to S3.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Streams with an EC2 Auto Scaling group enriching before S3 PutObject.
cards.why: Firehose is fully managed batching with Lambda transform; EC2 fleet adds cost and operations.

cards.scenario: Migrate Java app and MongoDB unchanged, similar architecture, high availability for both.
cards.ok: EC2 Auto Scaling across AZs + Multi-AZ Amazon DocumentDB with MongoDB compatibility.
cards.bad: DocumentDB in a single Availability Zone deployment.
cards.why: Single-AZ DocumentDB fails the high availability requirement for the database tier.

cards.scenario: Checkout must survive a massive sale surge; social login; most scalable.
cards.ok: Cognito social login, ALB + Auto Scaling web tier, SQS buffer, DynamoDB storage.
cards.bad: Web servers on ELB writing purchases directly to DynamoDB without a queue.
cards.why: SQS decouples the surge from the datastore writes; the direct-write version has no buffer.

cards.scenario: IoT data stopped updating DynamoDB; troubleshoot device connectivity.
cards.ok: Register devices with IoT Device Management; monitor health and connection to IoT Core.
cards.bad: IoT Device Defender to add the certificate authority and establish connectivity.
cards.why: Device Defender audits security and detects anomalies; it does not troubleshoot connectivity.

cards.scenario: Durable, highly available, scalable global news site (select two).
cards.ok: RDS Multi-AZ with Read Replicas + S3 for media; CloudFront CDN for global delivery.
cards.bad: Oracle RAC on RDS with Read Replicas.
cards.why: Oracle RAC is not supported in RDS; EBS RAID 0 is less durable than S3.

cards.scenario: Lambda throttled and DynamoDB throughput exceeded as meters grow (select two).
cards.ok: Raise DynamoDB WCU + put Kinesis data stream behind API Gateway to batch.
cards.bad: Raise API Gateway stage throttling limits and burst capacity.
cards.why: Errors come from Lambda and DynamoDB limits, not API Gateway throttling.

cards.scenario: What happens to the RDS Multi-AZ database during failover?
cards.ok: CNAME record changes from primary to standby.
cards.bad: The IP address of the primary is switched to the standby.
cards.why: The endpoint CNAME is repointed to the promoted standby; no new instance, no reboot.

cards.scenario: Queue photo-processing jobs, scale workers cheaply, archive afterwards.
cards.ok: SQS queue-depth Auto Scaling of Spot workers, then Glacier archive.
cards.bad: SNS passes job messages; CloudWatch terminates idle Spot workers; archive to Glacier.
cards.why: SNS cannot hold jobs for processing; S3 IA is not archival.

cards.scenario: Replace email-based order shipping process with automated workflow.
cards.ok: Orders in DynamoDB; Step Functions workflow per order marks status and prints label.
cards.bad: SQS queue polled by scheduled Lambda every 5 minutes; SNS on shipment.
cards.why: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step order stages with state; scheduled polling is clunky.

cards.scenario: Keep Oracle-backed news site available if database server fails.
cards.ok: RDS Oracle with Multi-AZ deployments.
cards.bad: RDS Oracle with Read Replicas.
cards.why: Writers need a writable database; Read Replicas cannot take writes after failure.

cards.scenario: Process visitor clickstream in real time to build user analytics.
cards.ok: Push clicks by session to Kinesis; analyze with Kinesis workers.
cards.bad: Logs to S3 analyzed with EMR.
cards.why: EMR batch analysis is not real-time; Kinesis handles streaming data.

cards.scenario: 1,000 TB POSIX block storage on-premises; users still need partial access during backup.
cards.ok: Gateway Cached Volumes (up to 1,024 TB, hot data kept locally).
cards.bad: Gateway Stored Volumes from Storage Gateway.
cards.why: Stored volumes cap at 512 TB; cached volumes support 1,024 TB with frequently used data local.

cards.scenario: Versioning enabled after four files existed; two later updated, one new file added.
cards.ok: Untouched EUR and ASIA files keep null Version ID + updated files have two versions, first null.
cards.bad: Latest Version ID of NA and LA files is null.
cards.why: Pre-versioning objects get null ID; updates after enabling versioning get alphanumeric IDs, so latest is not null.

cards.scenario: DR site 250+ miles away with RTO 5 minutes, RPO 1 hour, minimum cost.
cards.ok: Warm standby: scaled-down running stacks and replicated standby database in backup region.
cards.bad: Pilot light with a large standby database and CloudFormation to build servers on demand.
cards.why: Pilot light must provision servers during failover and cannot meet the 5-minute RTO.

cards.scenario: Oracle volume for infrequently accessed historical data; most cost-effective, throughput-oriented.
cards.ok: Database Migration Service with a Cold HDD (sc1) volume.
cards.bad: AWS Transform MGN migration using Throughput Optimized (st1) volume.
cards.why: sc1 is cheaper for infrequent access; DMS is the database migration tool.

cards.scenario: Cut recording storage costs and automate transcription of NFS call recordings.
cards.ok: S3 with Glacier lifecycle at 90 days, Lambda starting Amazon Transcribe, serverless web portal.
cards.bad: S3 with Lambda trigger starting transcription via AWS IQ, portal on EC2 Auto Scaling.
cards.why: Transcribe automates speech-to-text; AWS IQ is a marketplace for human experts.

cards.scenario: Migrate 40 TB in 3 months over slow link; minimal downtime for critical VMs.
cards.ok: MGN for mission-critical VMs; others via Data Transfer Terminal to S3, then VM Import/Export.
cards.bad: 1 Gbps Direct Connect plus MGN for all VMs.
cards.why: Direct Connect works but is costly; Data Transfer Terminal avoids upgrading the slow Internet link.

cards.scenario: Move to managed RDS and managed app platform; most cost-effective strategy.
cards.ok: Replatform (lift, tinker, shift).
cards.bad: Refactor / re-architect.
cards.why: Replatform makes few cloud optimizations; refactor costs more time, effort and budget.

cards.scenario: Reduce downtime, discover PII in S3, cut cost of aging photos.
cards.ok: Macie for PII + lifecycle to S3 IA after a month + RDS Multi-AZ.
cards.bad: Inspector for PII, lifecycle to Glacier Deep Archive, RDS Multi-AZ.
cards.why: Macie classifies S3 PII; Inspector does vulnerability scanning, not data discovery.

cards.scenario: Meet 2-hour RTO and 10-minute RPO for trading database (select two).
cards.ok: Hourly backups plus 5-minute logs to S3 with CRR; AWS Backup continuous PITR.
cards.bad: 15-minute backups stored in Glacier with 5-minute logs in S3.
cards.why: Glacier retrieval takes hours and misses RTO; instance store is ephemeral.

cards.scenario: DR for on-prem JBoss and Oracle CMS with best RTO.
cards.ok: EC2 for JBoss and Oracle, restore RMAN backups from S3, EBS volume from Storage Gateway.
cards.bad: Restore RMAN backups from Glacier onto RDS Oracle with EBS static content.
cards.why: Glacier restores are slow, and RDS Oracle does not support RMAN.

cards.scenario: Plan large on-prem to AWS migration (select three).
cards.ok: Transform discovery tool + Transform migration assessment + CART readiness report.
cards.bad: Use AWS Transform MGN to automate the migration.
cards.why: MGN performs migration, not planning; X-Ray and Inspector do not assess migration readiness.

cards.scenario: Speed up worldwide uploads of large photos to a central S3 bucket.
cards.ok: S3 Transfer Acceleration via the s3-accelerate endpoint.
cards.bad: Multipart upload to the same S3 bucket.
cards.why: Multipart parallelizes but distant users still face the slow Internet path.

cards.scenario: Protect Volume Gateway iSCSI from replay attacks.
cards.ok: Configure CHAP to authenticate iSCSI initiator connections.
cards.bad: Configure CHAP to authenticate NFS connections.
cards.why: CHAP protects iSCSI against playback attacks; it does not apply to NFS.

cards.scenario: Describe how SSE-S3 protects data at rest.
cards.ok: Each object encrypted with a unique key, itself encrypted by a regularly rotated master key.
cards.bad: SSE-S3 lets you manage the KMS keys while S3 does the encryption.
cards.why: SSE-S3 is fully S3-managed AES-256; managing KMS keys is SSE-KMS, not SSE-S3.

cards.scenario: Only cybersecurity team may access the ACM X.509 certificate; DevOps manages EC2.
cards.ok: IAM policy restricting certificate store access to cybersecurity team; terminate SSL on the ELB.
cards.bad: SCP limiting certificate store access to cybersecurity, plus SSL termination on the ELB.
cards.why: IAM policy grants the access control here; terminating SSL on the ELB keeps the private key off EC2.

cards.scenario: Each scientist sees only own files in shared S3 bucket; monthly access audit reports.
cards.ok: Identity Center permission set with aws:PrincipalTag prefix + CloudTrail S3 data events queried by Athena.
cards.bad: S3 server access logging with logs stored in EMRFS, queried by Athena.
cards.why: CloudTrail data events record who accessed which object; EMRFS log storage is not valid for server access logs.

cards.scenario: Grant third-party AWS organization least-privilege API/CLI access to our resources.
cards.ok: Third party supplies External ID; we create role with that External ID in its trust policy.
cards.bad: Create IAM role and let the third party assume it via STS.
cards.why: External ID prevents the confused deputy problem; a plain role trust lacks it.

cards.scenario: Add HTTPS to ALB-fronted site, most cost-effective and easiest.
cards.ok: Free ACM public certificate attached to the Application Load Balancer.
cards.bad: ACM private certificate configured on the ALB.
cards.why: Public ACM certificates are free; private CA adds monthly fees.

cards.scenario: Keep SSL private key secure; logs decryptable by few users.
cards.ok: TCP load balancing on ELB + CloudHSM SSL offload + logs to private S3 with SSE.
cards.bad: Same CloudHSM setup, but logs on ephemeral volume with random AES key.
cards.why: CloudHSM holds the key; ephemeral volume is temporary, not durable log storage.

cards.scenario: Mitigate DDoS on a single-VPC trading platform and notify team (select two).
cards.ok: AWS WAF custom rules + Shield Advanced DDoS detection and monitoring.
cards.bad: Network Firewall rule-based filtering.
cards.why: Network Firewall centrally manages rules across many VPCs and accounts; this is one VPC.

cards.scenario: Store and retrieve DB password securely; rotate every 60 days.
cards.ok: Secrets Manager secret; app retrieves at launch; dynamic reference for MasterUserPassword.
cards.bad: Secrets Manager secret passed to instance via UserData with Ref.
cards.why: UserData and Ref expose the secret; dynamic reference plus runtime retrieval keeps it protected.

cards.scenario: Sync on-premises patch baselines to EC2 and automate patch schedule, least effort.
cards.ok: Patch Manager with baselines, SSM Agent on instances, scheduling via Maintenance Windows.
cards.bad: Patch Manager scheduled with Lambda jobs and Run Command.
cards.why: Maintenance Windows is the built-in scheduler; custom Lambda scheduling adds needless effort.

cards.scenario: Give a compliance auditor access to AWS resource logs.
cards.ok: Enable CloudTrail logging; create read-only IAM user for the auditor.
cards.bad: Create IAM role for the auditor and attach it to EC2, S3, and DynamoDB.
cards.why: Roles attach to resources that assume them, not to external auditors; CloudTrail plus read-only access suits audits.

cards.scenario: Auto-recover EC2 on hardware failure keeping same IP address.
cards.ok: CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with EC2 recover action.
cards.bad: Elastic IP plus alarm that stops and starts the instance.
cards.why: Recover action keeps instance ID, private IP and Elastic IP; stop/start loses ephemeral state.
